strengths: Rigorous verification methodology: the paper goes beyond typical search-based discovery work by proving error bounds on the discovered real-valued programs using interval arithmetic (Supplementary S2, Table S1), and by exhaustively testing float-valued programs over all float32 inputs, including checks against double-rounding with exact rational ground truth. This makes the central claim ('evolved programs beat mathematical baselines') solidly supported rather than merely sampled.

Strong and fair baselines: the comparison set spans Taylor, Padé, Chebyshev, three continued fractions, Remez minimax, and a modern lattice-reduction method (Sollya fpminimax), with baselines given favorable treatments (Horner form for FMA fusion, lattice-reduced float coefficients). Beating these by orders of magnitude in precision per operation count is a genuinely meaningful result.

The float32 case study is practically interesting and well analyzed: the 3x+ speedup is explained mechanistically via XLA's CPU Parallel Task Assigner and fusion passes (Supplementary S3), transfer across a decade of Intel/AMD CPUs is measured, and the authors are appropriately candid that the speed results are compiler- and setting-specific.

The 'zero knowledge' framing is honestly executed: the method uses only field operations, starts from identity programs, and the evolutionary machinery (GP compute graphs + CMA-ES inner loop + distributed NSGA-II variant) is described in enough detail (Methods 2-4, hyperparameters, stopping rules, mutation probabilities) to be reproducible in principle.

Honest treatment of limitations: bloat, junk code, compute cost (one billion samples, datacenter scale), compiler-version sensitivity, and the open question of whether more sophisticated symbolic regression methods would do better at scale are all discussed directly in the Discussion rather than hidden.

Extension beyond the exponential (log2, erf, Airy) with attention to the distinct failure modes of baselines (relative-error singularities, wavy functions) strengthens the generality claim beyond a single cherry-picked function.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited. The components are all standard (genetic programming over compute graphs à la Koza, CMA-ES coefficient optimization, NSGA-II multi-objective selection). The distributed variant dNSGA-II is a plausible engineering contribution but incremental; the paper's value rests mainly on the scale of the search and the discovered artifacts rather than on a new algorithmic idea.

The headline float32 speedup is essentially an exploitation of a specific XLA compiler heuristic (dispatch routing/fusion decisions) that is acknowledged to be version- and setting-specific. While this is the point of end-to-end optimization, it somewhat weakens the 'discovered better mathematics' narrative for the practical case, and the paper itself concedes the mechanism is an artifact of compiler internals.

Compute cost and efficiency of the search are not characterized: the paper does not report how many days/cores were consumed, nor any ablation showing which design choices (e.g., dNSGA-II vs. simpler selection, CMA-ES vs. Levenberg-Marquardt) actually matter. 'A few days and reproducibly' is asserted but not quantified.

No comparison against modern learned search methods (e.g., RL-based expression discovery, transformer-based symbolic regression) even in a limited setting; the claim of 'first to discover state-of-the-art mathematical algorithms through evolutionary search' is plausible but the positioning against the closest competitors is left as future work.

Precision beyond ~3 for erf and the restriction to 4 field operations (no FMA, bit shifts, or integer ops in the search space) bound the practical reach of the method; the extension section is more a demonstration than a systematic evaluation. No code release is explicitly promised, which would limit reproducibility of the search itself (though the discovered programs and verification procedures are fully specified).

strengths: Rigorous verification methodology: the paper distinguishes between search-time approximations (finite validation sets, approximate ground truth) and final testing, proving real-valued error bounds via interval arithmetic (Supplementary S2, Table S1) and exhaustively evaluating float32 precision over all possible values, including a check for double-rounding effects against an exact-rational-arithmetic ground truth. This is unusually careful for symbolic regression work.

The core claim of the real-valued results (Figure 1) is a mathematically proven gap: evolved programs are given proven upper bounds on error while baselines receive lower-bound estimates, so the orders-of-magnitude precision advantage is well supported.

The float32 case study is honest about its specificity: the paper clearly states the >3x speedup is a compiler-specific effect, then explains the root cause in detail (Supplementary S3 traces it to XLA's Fusion and CPU Parallel Task Assigner passes) and demonstrates transfer across a decade of CPU architectures (Figure 5).

The paper situates its contribution honestly relative to AlphaTensor/AlphaDev-style RL discoveries, superoptimization [51], and classical symbolic regression, and includes a candid limitations discussion (bloat, compute cost, slow evolution beyond precision ~3 for erf, specificity of results).

The method itself is simple and the algorithmic components (dNSGA-II, CMA-ES coefficient optimization, graph mutations) are described in enough detail (Methods 2-4, hyperparameters) to assess and reimplement.
weaknesses: Generality of the contribution is thin relative to the title and framing. The paper claims 'State-of-the-Art Mathematical Functions,' but nearly all quantitative evidence is for the exponential (well-studied with strong baselines); the log2, erf, and Airy results are briefly reported with weaker baselines (e.g., log2 baselines reportedly never reaching under 3 ULP, which seems implausibly weak given that production libm log2f implementations achieve <1 ULP) and with estimated, not proven, precision.

The headline 3x float32 speedup is substantially an artifact of a single XLA compiler version's parallel-task-assignment heuristic (missing a dispatch function), rather than of a genuinely faster computation. The paper acknowledges this and calls it a case study, but it weakens the practical significance claim and the result may not survive compiler upgrades; sensitivity to compiler version is not measured.

Compute cost is a serious limitation that is under-quantified: the search uses 10^4 CPU cores for up to one billion evaluated programs, each requiring XLA compilation and CMA-ES coefficient optimization. No wall-clock, energy, or cost figures are given, making it impossible to assess the 'Immediate Cost, Long-term Gain' argument (Section 3.4) quantitatively.

Fairness of baselines is uneven: real-valued baselines are a well-chosen suite (Taylor, Padé, Chebyshev, Remez minimax, continued fractions, lattice reduction), but for the float case the comparison is against JAX-compiled polynomial/rational expressions rather than against actual production math libraries (e.g., glibc or Intel MKL expf), which are the true practitioners' alternative.

Reproducibility is questionable: there is no statement of code or artifact release, and the results depend on a specific JAX/Jaxlib/XLA version (0.4.11), specific compiler heuristics, and timing noise mitigations. The discoveries themselves are released in the paper, but the search process is not.

The methodological novelty is limited: distributed NSGA-II with sampling-based selection, CMA-ES coefficient fitting, and graph mutation operators are all straightforward combinations of well-known techniques; the contribution is the scale and domain of application rather than a new algorithm, which is legitimate but narrows the audience.

Some claims are under-supported, e.g., 'no proof of optimality' claims aside, statements like 'these detailed considerations were not needed' for the log2 case, and the transferability discussion ('more a statement about the similarity of these architectures') are qualitative; also references [33] and [19] for CMA-ES are inconsistent, and citing Wikipedia [67] for ULP convention is not appropriate for a venue like ICML.

strengths: The central claim — that a simple evolutionary method can discover approximation programs matching or beating centuries of mathematical work for a fixed precision/operation budget — is unusually well verified: the real-valued results are backed by proven error bounds via interval arithmetic (Supplementary S2, Table S1), so the headline 'orders of magnitude better precision' gap in Figure 1 is mathematically established rather than merely observed.

The float32 case study is evaluated exhaustively (error measured over all possible float32 values, double-rounding effects checked against exact rational-arithmetic ground truth), and speed measurements use interleaved repeated timing to avoid selection bias — this is a level of numerical rigor rare in ML papers.

The baselines are strong and diverse (Taylor/Padé in Horner form, Remez minimax via Mathematica, Sollya's lattice-reduction fpminimax, continued fractions, Chebyshev), representing genuine state-of-the-art rather than strawmen.

The paper is honest and precise about the nature of its results: the speedup is explicitly framed as compiler- and hardware-specific (a case study), the transfer result to other CPUs is described as 'more a statement about the similarity of these architectures', and Supplementary S3 gives a convincing mechanistic explanation (fused-computation splitting and the CPU Parallel Task Assigner pass) for the 3x speedup.

The discovery of genuinely novel, interpretable programs (e.g., the 10-operation rational expression reusing intermediate results, Figure 2) with proofs that they are pole-free and well-defined on [0,1] constitutes a real contribution to the numerical methods literature, not just a machine learning demonstration.

Related work is thorough and places the contribution carefully relative to AutoML-Zero, AlphaTensor/AlphaDev, symbolic regression, and superoptimization; limitations (compute cost, slow evolution beyond precision ~3 for erf, compiler-specificity) are discussed candidly.
weaknesses: The computational cost of the search is not quantified. The paper mentions 10^4 workers, 10^9 samples, and 'a few days' of compute, but no wall-clock or core-hour figures are given, making it hard to assess the practicality of the 'immediate cost, long-term gain' argument in Section 3.4.

The 3x float32 speedup, while a striking case study, is essentially an exploitation of a specific XLA compilation artifact (the parallel task assigner dispatch overhead). The paper argues hand-engineering this is impractical, but it does not report whether trivial mitigations for the baselines (e.g., forcing fusion structure) were attempted; as presented, the win is against baselines that are knowingly mis-compiled, which somewhat qualifies its practical significance.

No code or artifact release is mentioned. Given that the results are tied to specific versions of JAX/Jaxlib/XLA (0.4.11) and that reproducibility of an evolutionary search at this scale is a serious concern, the lack of a stated release path is a notable gap.

The extension to other transcendental functions (log, erf, Airy) is evidence-level only: for erf and Airy, precisions are estimated from 1M-point sampling without the interval-arithmetic proofs applied to the exponential, and no baselines beyond Taylor/Padé/Chebyshev are attempted for those functions.

There is no comparison against modern large-scale symbolic regression or RL-based program search methods applied to this task; the paper acknowledges this as an open question, but some evidence that the simple evolutionary approach is the right tool (versus, e.g., learned proposal distributions) would strengthen the methodological claim.

Minor presentation issues: several typos ('what we ultimate care about', 'mimize', 'indepedent'), and Figure 1 mixes proven bounds (evolved) with sampled estimates (baselines) on the same axes — the direction of the argument is sound, but per-operation-count baseline curves could be made tighter with the same interval-arithmetic machinery.

The speed objective is measured as throughput in an embarrassingly parallel regime with a fixed stack depth, an evaluation setup chosen partly to prevent compile-away; sensitivity of the reported speedups to this benchmark harness is not explored.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated hypothesis: optimizing for finite-precision targets can yield more efficient transcendental function approximations, and the paper provides a rigorous test of it.

The headline result is convincing and unusually rigorous for a program-search paper: the 10-operation exponential program exceeds known approximations of comparable size by many orders of magnitude, and the accuracy of evolved programs is established with mathematically proven error bounds (interval arithmetic via IBEX for real-valued programs; Gappa with IEEE-754 rounding semantics and exhaustive evaluation for the float32 case), while baseline accuracy is an overestimate — so the Pareto comparison in Figure 4 is conservative and mathematically certain.

Careful, strong baselines: Taylor (Horner form), Pade, Chebyshev, continued fractions (Euler, Gauss, Macon), and Remez minimax polynomials/rational functions, with lattice-reduction (Sollya) treatment for the hardware-aware case. The authors also present an honest negative result (erf, Section 4.5) where Pade beats their method at higher accuracies.

Broad empirical coverage across five diverse target functions with different challenges (zeros in the domain, oscillatory behavior, non-analytic behavior near 0), plus a hardware-aware extension demonstrating a >3x speedup and cross-architecture transfer over 8 years of Intel/AMD hardware.

Useful ablations (Section 4.8) showing that the population selection (dNSGA-II), the CMA-ES coefficient inner loop, and the graph-based mutations each contribute meaningfully, and an interesting observation of convergent evolution across independent runs.

Good reproducibility posture: open-sourced code, proofs scripts, detailed appendices (search space, mutation probabilities, CMA-ES and dNSGA-II hyperparameters, compute budget of ~6k-9.6k core-days), and an honest limitations section (range reduction assumption, compute cost, interpretability-quality tradeoff).

The discovered programs themselves (e.g., the nested-power rational form and the compiler-path exploit yielding near-exact float32 exponentials) represent genuinely novel mathematical/programming artifacts, verified rather than merely claimed.
weaknesses: The method is an assembly of well-known components (GP with graph mutations, NSGA-II, CMA-ES); the contribution lies in the application, system integration, and discovered artifacts rather than algorithmic novelty. The paper acknowledges this, but the ML-methodological advance is modest.

Scale of evidence is limited: only five target functions, all classical, and all evaluated via the same standard range-reduction framework. The claim that symbolic regression 'discovers state-of-the-art mathematical functions' is well supported for these cases, but generalization to a wider class of functions or to settings without convenient range reduction remains untested.

Very high computational cost (100-10k processes for 1-4 days; thousands of core-days per function) with no systematic analysis of sample efficiency, scaling behavior, or variance across budgets beyond limited repeats; practical adoption is gated on substantial cluster resources.

Some experimental details leave questions: the accuracy estimate during search uses random finite samples, and while held-out testing (A.10) mitigates this for reported results, the tiered verification rigor means many plotted points rest on lighter empirical checks than the headline results.

The hardware-aware speedup depends on a specific XLA/JAX compiler heuristic (the Parallel Task Assigner); while transfer across CPUs is shown, the result is tied to one compiler stack and could be brittle across toolchain versions.

The relationship to LLM-based program discovery (e.g., FunSearch) is not experimentally compared; given that these are the most prominent current alternatives for program search from scratch, some discussion or comparison would strengthen positioning.

strengths: Rigorous verification: the authors mathematically prove error bounds for their most important discovered programs using interval arithmetic (IBEX) and the Gappa prover, including a sub-1-ULP guarantee for the float32 hardware-aware program; evolved-program accuracies are reported as conservative lower bounds while baseline accuracies are upper bounds, which makes the headline claim (e.g., 10-operation exponential exceeding prior approximations by orders of magnitude) mathematically certain rather than empirically suggestive.

Thorough, honest evaluation: baselines were chosen to be strong (Chebyshev, Pade, Remez minimax, continued fractions), the authors report cases where baselines win (erf at higher accuracies), include a hand-designed tailored baseline for the Bessel function, test on unseen points to guard against overfitting, and run ablations of each algorithmic stage showing each component contributes.

Interesting demonstration of the core hypothesis that finite-precision targets change the optimization landscape, including evidence of intermediate-value reuse and convergent evolution across independent runs, and a hardware-aware section showing >3x speedups that transfer across 8 years of Intel/AMD hardware.

Reproducibility is addressed: code is open-sourced, discovered programs are listed in the appendix, hyperparameters, compute budgets, and search details are documented extensively (Appendices A.1-A.10, B).
weaknesses: The 'zero-knowledge' framing is overstated. Substantial mathematical knowledge is injected around the search: range reduction is assumed and applied identically to all baselines, the sqrt operation is added specifically because the authors know the Bessel function behaves like sqrt(x) near zero, domains and error metrics (relative vs. absolute) are chosen per-function with knowledge of each function's analytic structure, and CMA-ES coefficient optimization is far from knowledge-free. The search itself is 'zero-knowledge', but the overall system is not, and the paper's framing risks overstating the contribution.

Methodological novelty is limited. The paper explicitly combines well-established components (genetic programming with graph mutations, a distributed variant of NSGA-II, CMA-ES inner-loop optimization, standard interval-arithmetic proof techniques) without proposing a new search algorithm; the contribution is primarily an empirical demonstration on a narrow task, and the authors acknowledge this. The claim of being 'first to discover state-of-the-art mathematical algorithms through evolutionary search' rests on a specific reading of prior work (e.g., stochastic superoptimization, FunSearch-style LLM-based discovery) that deserves more careful comparison; no RL- or LLM-based discovery baseline is compared against despite the paper citing that literature.

Extreme computational cost with unclear cost-effectiveness: 100-10k cores for 1-4 days per target (6-9.6k core-days for the headline result). The amortization argument for one-time cost is reasonable, but there is no analysis of how accuracy scales with compute budget, no comparison of evolved solutions against much cheaper search strategies at matched budgets, and no evidence that the approach generalizes beyond the six carefully chosen target functions.

The hardware-aware speedup result, while technically impressive, is of limited practical value: the >3x speedup arises from triggering an unintended compiler dispatch path in the XLA Parallel Task Assigner, which the authors themselves note would be 'impractical' to write by hand and is specific to one compiler stack. This is an intriguing artifact of black-box search rather than a broadly deployable numerical improvement.

Scope of empirical support is narrow: six transcendental functions, chosen a priori to present specific challenges, with only the exponential function receiving full mathematical proofs for the whole Pareto front; claims of generality (extensibility to other functions, operation sets, objectives) remain speculative.

Some aspects of baseline construction could be contested (e.g., Remez optimization initialized by rational fitting, Horner-form constraints to encourage FMA emission), and although the authors argue these choices give baselines their best chance, systematic verification that baselines are not handicapped by implementation choices is limited.

strengths: Compelling central finding: a zero-knowledge evolutionary search starting from empty programs discovers programs for transcendental functions that provably exceed well-established baselines (Taylor, Pade, Chebyshev, minimax, continued fractions) at matched operation counts, with the flagship result being a 10-operation exponential approximation beating known approximations of the same size by many orders of magnitude.

Unusual rigor for an evolutionary-computation paper: the headline claims are backed by mathematically proven error bounds (interval arithmetic via IBEX for real-valued programs; Gappa for float32 programs with a proven <1 ULP bound), and the paper carefully explains why evolved accuracy is an underestimate while baseline accuracy is an overestimate, making the comparison gap mathematically certain rather than merely empirical.

Exhaustive and fair baseline treatment: the authors enumerate the strongest baselines they could identify (including hand-tailored Frobenius-based baselines for the Bessel case), present results 'without excluding cases due to search failure,' and honestly report cases where baselines win (e.g., erf at higher accuracies).

Useful ablations (population selection, CMA-ES inner loop, mutations vs. random graphs) that justify each methodological component, plus interesting scientific observations such as convergent evolution across independent runs and the discovery of unconventional non-polynomial/non-rational forms.

The hardware-aware extension (Section 4.6) is a genuinely novel angle: evolving programs that exploit real float32 rounding and even compiler compilation-path artifacts to achieve >3x speedups, with the speedups shown to transfer across 8 years of Intel/AMD hardware; the compiler-dispatch explanation in Appendix C is a nice piece of forensic analysis.

Clear writing, good figures, thorough appendices (search details, compute budget disclosure of ~6k core-days, released code), and an honest limitations section covering range-reduction reliance, compute cost, and the interpretability-quality tradeoff.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest: the system is a competent combination of existing techniques (genetic programming on compute graphs, a distributed NSGA-II variant, CMA-ES coefficient optimization). The contribution is primarily an empirical/systems demonstration rather than a new search algorithm, which some readers may view as engineering rather than a methodological advance.

Very high compute cost (100-10k processes for 1-4 days; 6k core-days for the main result) limits reproducibility in practice and raises questions about whether classical methods with comparable compute budgets (e.g., global optimization of rational function coefficients beyond the tested configurations) were fully explored.

Scope of evaluation is limited to five target functions plus one hardware-aware variant; generalization to a broader benchmark of functions, and comparison against a broader set of modern automated approximation tools or learning-based methods, is not demonstrated.

The hardware-aware speedup partially depends on incidental compiler behavior (the XLA parallel task assigner heuristics), which the authors themselves note would be 'impractical' to engineer by hand; this makes the practical durability of that particular result fragile across compiler versions, even though accuracy results transfer.

Some details that could affect comparisons are only sketched in the main text (e.g., sample sizes for accuracy estimation, tuning of baseline polynomial orders, the tiered verification protocol), requiring careful reading of appendices; a skeptical reader may want stronger guarantees that baselines received equivalent optimization effort to evolved programs.

Claim of being the first to discover state-of-the-art mathematical algorithms through evolution is asserted carefully but rests on a specific definition of 'state-of-the-art' (accuracy at fixed operation count under range reduction); the framing could be scrutinized.
